summary: Describes current best security practice for OAuth 2.0. It updates and extends the threat model and advice in RFC 6749, RFC 6750 and RFC 6819 to reflect experience gained since, covers new threats, and deprecates some modes of operation considered less secure.

eli5.summary: OAuth is how apps get limited permission to use your accounts. After years of trouble, this lists safer habits and says to stop some risky shortcuts.

subtitle: The rulebook of OAuth 2.0 security advice learned the hard way, including which risky shortcuts to stop using.

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 spread into banking, health and other high-security uses and into dynamic setups it was not designed for, and attackers kept exploiting known weak implementation patterns.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects current best practice: exact redirect URI matching, PKCE for the authorization code grant, mix-up and CSRF defenses, sender-constrained and audience-restricted tokens, and no implicit or password grants. It also sets out an updated attacker model and walks through each attack with its countermeasures.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 6749, RFC 6750 and RFC 6819 without replacing them, and says OAuth 2.1 will incorporate its recommendations. Following it may break interoperability with older ecosystems.

today: RFC 9700 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 240) from January 2025 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 6749, RFC 6750 and RFC 6819, and the text says OAuth 2.1, then under development, will incorporate its security recommendations.

sections.title: Why a Security Update Was Needed
sections.content:
OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749, RFC 6750) became the standard for API protection and the basis for federated login using OpenID Connect. RFC 9700 lists four reasons the original advice was no longer enough.

  • Known implementation weaknesses and anti-patterns keep being attacked, even though most are covered in the threat model of RFC 6819.
  • OAuth is used where security needs are higher than first assumed, such as open banking, eHealth, eGovernment and electronic signatures.
  • Relationships are more dynamic. OAuth first assumed that clients knew their servers' URLs at deployment time. Today the same client may talk to different providers, which Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) and Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414) were developed to support.
  • Technology changed. For example, the way browsers treat fragments when redirecting has changed, and with it the security model of the implicit grant.

The document adds new requirements, deprecates some modes of operation as less secure or even insecure, and complements rather than replaces the older security advice. It admits that following it may break interoperability, but it is RECOMMENDED that implementers upgrade as soon as feasible.
sections.eli5: When the first OAuth rules were written, nobody knew all the tricks bad guys would try. This is the updated safety guide, like adding new rules to a game after players found loopholes.

sections.title: The Core Best Practices
sections.content:
Section 2 is the short list every OAuth implementer should know. The main points:

  • Exact redirect matching. Authorization servers MUST compare redirection URIs with exact string matching, except for variable port numbers in localhost redirection URIs of native apps.
  • No open redirectors. Clients and authorization servers MUST NOT expose URLs that forward the browser to arbitrary URIs taken from a query parameter.
  • CSRF protection. Clients MUST prevent cross-site request forgery, using PKCE, the OpenID Connect nonce, or one-time state values bound to the user agent.
  • Mix-up defense. When a client can talk to more than one authorization server, a defense is REQUIRED, preferably the iss parameter from RFC 9207.
  • PKCE. Public clients MUST use PKCE (RFC 7636) with the authorization code grant. For confidential clients it is RECOMMENDED. Authorization servers MUST support it, and clients SHOULD use a method that does not expose the verifier in the request. Currently only S256 qualifies.
  • No implicit grant. Clients SHOULD NOT use the implicit grant or other response types that issue access tokens in the authorization response. They should use the code response type.
  • No password grant. The resource owner password credentials grant MUST NOT be used, because it exposes the user's credentials to the client and does not suit two-factor or multi-step authentication.
  • Limited tokens. Access tokens SHOULD be sender-constrained and restricted to the minimum privileges and to specific resource servers. Refresh tokens for public clients MUST be sender-constrained or use rotation.
  • Strong client authentication. Asymmetric methods such as mutual TLS (RFC 8705) or signed JWTs are RECOMMENDED, so servers need not store sensitive symmetric keys.

It also requires that authorization responses never travel over unencrypted connections, so the http scheme is not allowed for redirection URIs except for loopback redirection by native clients. CORS MAY be supported at the token endpoint and similar endpoints but MUST NOT be supported at the authorization endpoint.
sections.eli5: Think of it as a short checklist for a secure clubhouse: check the guest's full name exactly, never leave a side door open, make sure each key only opens one door, and stop using the old password trick.

sections.title: The Updated Attacker Model
sections.content:
RFC 6819 assumed certain attackers without saying so. RFC 9700 makes the attacker model explicit and extends it to five kinds of attacker. The goal is to protect the authorization of a resource owner and the later use of the access token, as well as practically possible, at least against these attackers.

A1 and A2 match the minimal model used in formal analysis of OAuth. A web attacker (A1) can run endpoints, browsers and even registered clients and authorization servers, and can lure users to attacker-chosen URIs. A network attacker (A2) also controls the network and can eavesdrop, manipulate, spoof and block messages unless cryptography such as TLS protects them. A3 to A5 are narrower capabilities that typically occur together with A1 or A2, and attackers can collaborate. The RFC says implementers MUST take into account all possible types of attackers in their environment, not only these.

An attacker (A1) or (A2) can also be or act as a resource owner, for example using their own browser to replay tokens or codes obtained by other attacks.
sections.eli5: Before building a fence, you list who might try to climb it: a kid next door, someone watching from the street, or someone who found a spare key. This section is that list.

sections.title: Redirect URIs and Leaking Credentials
sections.content:
Several attacks target where the authorization response is sent and what it can reveal.

Insufficient redirect URI validation. Some servers let clients register patterns such as https://*.somesite.example/*. The RFC shows that a naive wildcard might accept https://attacker.example/.somesite.example, sending the code to the attacker. Even correct wildcards can fail if an attacker takes over a subdomain. With the implicit grant, a client that is an open redirector lets the browser reattach the URL fragment carrying the access token to an attacker's URL. The countermeasure is exact matching (simple string comparison as in RFC 3986), no open redirectors, and preferring the authorization code response type. Servers MAY also add an arbitrary fragment such as #_ to Location headers to stop fragment reattachment.

Referer header leakage. Codes, state values and sometimes tokens can leak through the HTTP Referer header from the client's or the authorization server's pages if they include third-party content or links. Pages that handle OAuth SHOULD NOT include third-party resources or links to external sites. Further measures include a Referrer Policy such as no-referrer, invalidating authorization codes after first use (with revocation of tokens previously issued if a code is redeemed twice), and using the form post response mode.

Browser history. Codes in redirect URLs and tokens in fragments or query strings can end up in the browser history. Clients MUST NOT pass access tokens in a URI query parameter as described in RFC 6750 section 2.3.
sections.eli5: If you hand someone a letter and the address on the envelope is only almost right, it can end up with a stranger. So check the address letter for letter, and do not leave the letter lying around where others can read it.

sections.title: Mix-Up, Injection, CSRF and PKCE Downgrade
sections.content:
Mix-up attacks. They can happen when a client talks to two or more authorization servers and at least one is under the attacker's control, for example through dynamic registration or a compromise. The client is tricked into sending a code or token for an honest server to the attacker's server. The defenses are for the client to remember which issuer it sent each request to, bound to the user agent, and then either compare the iss value in the response against it (and abort on mismatch), or use a distinct redirection URI for each issuer. The second defense SHOULD only be used if other options are not available, because an attacker may be able to circumvent it.

Authorization code injection. An attacker who has a stolen code starts their own session with the legitimate client and swaps the new code for the stolen one, linking the attacker's session to the victim's resources. Public clients are exposed more simply, since the attacker can use the stolen code at the token endpoint directly. The fix is to bind every code to one client instance and transaction, using PKCE or, for OpenID Connect, the nonce. The RFC notes the check only works if the client validates the nonce in the ID Token from the token endpoint and disregards all tokens until it succeeds.

Access token injection. With the implicit grant, an attacker can swap in a leaked access token. There is no way to detect this in pure OAuth flows, which is one reason the implicit grant is discouraged.

CSRF. The classic defense is a random state value tied to the user agent session. PKCE or the nonce gives the same protection, but a client MUST first make sure the server supports PKCE, otherwise it must use state or nonce.

PKCE downgrade. If a server supports PKCE but does not require it, an attacker can strip the code_challenge parameter in their own flow and hand the victim a code that is bound to no challenge. The server MUST therefore reject any token request containing a code_verifier when no code_challenge was present in the authorization request.
sections.eli5: A mix-up is like a trickster sending you to the wrong shop door so that your coupon ends up in his pocket. Defenses are checking the shop's name when you get back, and using a secret handshake that only you and the real shop know.

sections.title: Stolen Tokens and Refresh Tokens
sections.content:
Access tokens can leak from a resource server, for example when a client is tricked into sending a token to a counterfeit resource server or when a real one is compromised. The RFC therefore says authorization servers SHOULD make access tokens both sender-constrained and audience-restricted, noting that architecture and performance reasons may prevent this in some deployments. Resource servers MUST treat access tokens as sensitive secrets and not store or transfer them in plaintext.

A sender-constrained token only works for a sender that can prove it knows a secret. Two methods are in use: mutual TLS (RFC 8705), which compares the fingerprint of the client's public key, and DPoP (RFC 9449), an application-level proof based on a key pair. The RFC warns that this protection is weakened if an attacker gets both the token and the key material, as with corrupted client software or cross-site scripting in a browser.

Audience restriction ties a token to a particular resource server, which refuses a token meant for another audience. The client can tell the authorization server where it will use the token using RFC 8707 or the scope value. The RFC also discusses publishing lists of safe resource servers in metadata and rejects it as the main defense, because many clients do not implement security controls properly.

Refresh tokens represent the full scope of access, so they are an attractive target. Authorization servers MUST decide by risk assessment whether to issue them, and bind them to the scope and resource servers the owner consented to. For public clients they MUST use either sender-constrained refresh tokens or refresh token rotation: each refresh returns a new token and invalidates the old one, so if both attacker and client use a token, the server sees an invalidated one and revokes the active token. Refresh tokens SHOULD also expire after the client has been inactive for some time.
sections.eli5: A token is like a ticket. A ticket that only works for one person with their own ID, and only at one theater, is much harder to misuse if someone steals it. Refresh tickets get swapped for fresh ones each time so a copy stops working.

sections.title: Redirects, Proxies, Clickjacking and Browser Messages
sections.content:
The remaining attack classes mostly concern how servers and browsers handle redirects and framing.

  • Open redirection. Clients MUST NOT expose open redirectors. Authorization servers must also not redirect users to untrusted registered URIs after errors, a declined consent screen or a silent prompt=none request. They MUST authenticate the user first and SHOULD only redirect automatically to a trusted redirection URI.
  • 307 redirect. If an authorization server answers a login form POST with status 307, the browser may resend the user's credentials by POST to the client. Servers that redirect such requests MUST NOT use 307, and SHOULD use 303 (See Other) if HTTP redirection is used.
  • TLS terminating reverse proxies. A proxy MUST sanitize inbound requests so attackers cannot forge security-relevant headers such as X-Forwarded-For, and the link between proxy and application server MUST be protected against eavesdropping, injection and replay.
  • Client impersonating a resource owner. If client IDs and user identifiers share a namespace (like the sub claim in RFC 9068 tokens), authorization servers SHOULD NOT let clients choose their own client_id.
  • Clickjacking. Authorization servers MUST prevent it, using measures from RFC 6819 such as X-Frame-Options, and SHOULD also use Content Security Policy level 2 or greater.
  • In-browser communication. If postMessage carries the response, the server MUST send it to an explicit trusted client origin and never a wildcard origin, and the client MUST compare the sender origin with exact string matching.
sections.eli5: These are smaller doors a bad guy might sneak through: a signpost that points anywhere, a hallway where someone can swap the notes, or a fake button painted over the real one. Each gets its own lock.

items.label: Web attacker
items.desc: Runs arbitrary endpoints, browsers and servers, may operate registered clients, and can lure users to attacker-chosen URIs.

items.label: Network attacker
items.desc: Also controls the network: can eavesdrop, manipulate, spoof and block messages unless protected by cryptography such as TLS.

items.label: Reads authorization response
items.desc: Can read, but not modify, the authorization response, for example via open redirectors, mix-up attacks or browser history.

items.label: Reads authorization request
items.desc: Can read, but not modify, the authorization request.

items.label: Holds an access token
items.desc: Has acquired an access token, for example from a compromised or counterfeit resource server.

viz.caption: MIX-UP ATTACK ON THE AUTHORIZATION CODE GRANT

messages.label: Choose A-AS
messages.note: The user starts the grant using the attacker's server.

messages.label: Redirect to A-AS
messages.note: Client stores that A-AS was chosen and uses its client ID 666RVZJTA.

messages.label: 303 to H-AS
messages.note: Attacker swaps in the client's ID at H-AS, 7ZGZldHQ.

messages.label: Authorization request
messages.note: The user authorizes the client at H-AS.

messages.label: Redeem code
messages.note: The client still thinks A-AS issued it, so the attacker obtains the code.
